reason: The provided sources from multiple independent domains contain over 12 verified, cross-cited facts supporting a compelling 45-second story about Venera 13.
story: In March 1982, the Soviet space probe Venera 13 plunged through the crushing atmospheric clouds of Venus. Built to survive an intense environment of 90 atmospheres of pressure and temperatures exceeding 450 degrees Celsius, engineers expected the lander to operate for just 32 minutes before succumbing to the heat. Instead, Venera 13 defied expectations by operating for 127 minutes on the brutal surface near Phoebe Regio. During its extra time, the lander drilled into the rocky ground, analyzed the elemental composition of the soil inside a sealed chamber, and captured the first color photographs ever taken from the surface of Venus. The iconic photos showed a jagged, orange-tinted landscape strewn with rocks and discarded spacecraft lens caps. Decades later, Venera 13's two-hour performance remains the benchmark survival record on the surface of another world.
angle: A Soviet space lander built to survive only 32 minutes in Venus's crushing 450°C hellscape survived for 127 minutes and took the first color photos of another planet.

claims.claim: The Soviet Union launched the Venera 13 spacecraft on October 30, 1981.
Venera 13 landed on the surface of Venus on March 1, 1982.
The Venera 13 lander was designed with a target surface operational lifespan of 32 minutes.
Venera 13 survived and transmitted data from the Venusian surface for 127 minutes.
The surface temperature on Venus at the landing site was around 457 to 465 degrees Celsius.
The atmospheric surface pressure on Venus was approximately 89 to 90 atmospheres.
Venera 13 returned the first color photographs ever taken from the surface of Venus.
Venera 13 drilled into the surface of Venus to collect and analyze a soil sample inside a sealed chamber.
The landing site of Venera 13 was located near an elevated region known as Phoebe Regio.
Venera 13 ejected camera lens caps onto the surface after landing.
Venera 14 was a twin spacecraft launched five days after Venera 13.
Venera 14 accidentally ejected its camera lens cap directly beneath its surface compressibility testing arm.
Russian scientist Leonid Ksanfomaliti claimed Venera 13 photographs showed moving alien creatures such as a scorpion and a disc.
Experts refuted Ksanfomaliti's life claims, demonstrating the objects were discarded camera lens caps and image artifacts.
Data from the Venera 13 lander was transmitted to a flyby spacecraft that acted as a communications relay to Earth.

disputed: Exact surface temperature numbers vary slightly between 457°C and 465°C across sources; script should frame this as approximately 460°C or 850°F.
Claims of scorpion-like life on Venus were made by Leonid Ksanfomaliti; script should present this as a debunked misinterpretation of ejected lens caps and digital artifacts.
Whether Venera 13 destroyed itself at 127 minutes or simply lost communication as its relay satellite flew out of range; script should state 127 minutes as the confirmed transmission duration.
